description:
ROOTS is a multidisciplinary team using NASA Earth observations, geospatial intelligence, and AI to build practical solutions for resilient agriculture.
We transform space-based data into meaningful insights that help address real-world challenges and support a more resilient Earth.
summary:
Team Roots · NASA Space Apps 2026 · 
Challenge #06 “Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data”

Problem: Farmers repeat the same crop rotation while heat, water shortage and weak soil grow. In Faisalabad, about 505 mm of rain falls a year against about 1,800 mm of water demand.

Solution: A farmer picks their field on a map and answers four questions. The app then compares three rotations (existing, water-saving, soil-improvement) using 20 years of NASA data, in English, Urdu, Sindhi and Punjabi.

Key features:

Side-by-side rotation comparison: water, soil, nitrogen fixing, pest risk, best fit
Early-warning alerts, from Low to Critical, with what to do
What-If simulator for hotter and drier conditions
Live 7-day weather
AI assistant for farming questions only, with no fertilizer or pesticide doses

Data: NASA POWER (7,305 days of climate), NASA SMAP (soil moisture), NASA MODIS NDVI (vegetation), plus SoilGrids, FAO crop data, Open-Meteo and Gemini.

github repo: https://github.com/asifnawaz23/nasa_agroshift_AI
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

AgroShift AI is a free web app that helps farmers choose a better crop rotation for a changing climate using NASA Earth observation data. A farmer opens the app, picks their field on a satellite map (by search, GPS, a click, or one of our featured farms in Sindh, Punjab or Iowa), and answers four quick questions: current crop, soil type, water supply and their main goal (save water, improve soil, increase income, prevent erosion or reduce pests).

In a few seconds the app:

  1. Builds a 20-year climate profile of that location from 7,305 days of daily NASA POWER data (2006–2025): monthly temperature and rainfall, heat days above 35 °C and 40 °C, frost, 10-day dry spells, extreme rain and water demand (evapotranspiration, FAO-56 method). For featured farms it adds NASA SMAP satellite soil moisture and NASA MODIS NDVI vegetation greenness.
  2. Compares three rotations side by side: the farmer’s existing rotation, a water-saving rotation and a soil-improvement rotation. Each one shows climate suitability, yearly water need against rainfall, soil improvement, nitrogen-fixing crops, pest and disease risk, benefits, limitations and evidence with data sources. The best fit for the farmer’s goal is marked.
  3. Issues early-warning alerts (heat, drought, water deficit, frost, waterlogging, soil drying), graded Low to Critical. Each alert names the month, the crop and its growth stage, and a practical action.
  4. Runs What-If scenarios: sliders from −2 to +5 °C and −50% to +30% rain re-compute every score and alert in under a second, so farmers can test a hotter, drier future.
  5. Shows live weather: current conditions plus the next and last 7 days, with temperature and rainfall charts.
  6. Explains everything in plain language in English, Urdu, Sindhi and Punjabi, with an AI farm assistant that accepts typed or spoken questions.

How decisions are made: a transparent, rule-based engine, not a black-box model. It applies the FAO-56 water-balance method and crop growth-stage rules to NASA data, then weights six sub-scores (water fit, climate risk, soil health, erosion, pest break, income) by the farmer’s own priority. The AI only rewrites the engine’s numbers in simple words, so every result can be traced to a number and a source.

What benefits does it have?

  • Turns NASA data into a decision: farmers get a ranked, explained answer, not raw files or charts.
  • Saves water: for our Faisalabad farm, the water-saving rotation needs about 20% less water (1,125 mm instead of 1,400 mm a year), where rainfall is only about 505 mm.
  • Builds soil health: it shows which rotations add nitrogen-fixing legumes (chickpea, mungbean, berseem), cover the soil longer and break pest cycles.
  • Warns before damage: it shows the risky months. For example, cotton flowering in July meets about 17 days above 40 °C in Faisalabad.
  • Prepares for the future: the What-If test at +3 °C and −30% rain raises high alerts from 2 to 4, so farmers and advisors can plan ahead.
  • Accessible: free, no sign-up, works on a phone, in four languages, with voice input.

What is the intended impact?

Smallholder farmers in Pakistan and similar regions face rising heat, falling groundwater and declining soil, but rarely have access to climate data or agronomists. We want any farmer, extension worker or student to make evidence-based rotation choices that save water, protect soil and reduce climate losses, using the same NASA data scientists use. The tool is built to support farmer judgment and local experts, not replace them: every recommendation includes what to confirm with the local agriculture extension office.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Data: NASA POWER (daily point API), NASA SMAP (SPL3SMP_E) and NASA MODIS NDVI (MOD13Q1), both via NASA Earthdata AppEEARS; ISRIC SoilGrids; FAO crop water guidance (FAO-56, FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 33); Open-Meteo for the weather forecast.
  • Backend: Python, Django and Django REST Framework, pandas and NumPy, PostgreSQL (Neon), deployed on Render.
  • Frontend: JavaScript and React (Vite), Tailwind CSS, Leaflet maps (Esri satellite and OpenStreetMap tiles, Nominatim search), custom SVG charts and the browser Web Speech API for voice, deployed on Vercel.
  • AI: Google Gemini (free tier) for explanations and chat, with strict grounding and safety rules and a template fallback when it is unavailable.
  • Quality and tools: pytest and Django tests (160+ automated tests), Git and GitHub, VS Code, and AI coding assistants (Claude Code) for development support.
  • Hardware: none required. It runs in any web browser, on a laptop or a phone.

How is the project creative?

  • Explainable, not black-box: instead of training a model on data we don’t have, we encoded published agronomy science (FAO-56, crop stages, crop traits) so every score shows where it comes from.
  • “Same field, three futures”: farmers see their current rotation next to two alternatives, and with the What-If sliders they can see how each would hold up in a hotter, drier climate.
  • Crop-stage-aware alerts: a hot July matters only if a sensitive crop is flowering then. Our alerts connect NASA climate patterns to each crop’s calendar.
  • Local languages: full explanations and chat in Urdu, Sindhi and Punjabi, the languages farmers actually speak, with voice input.
  • Data checked against reality: we used MODIS NDVI to move our featured pins off towns and onto real cropland.

What factors did the team consider?

  • Scientific validity: standard methods (FAO-56), 20 years of data, and honest labels on every value: Historical (NASA record), Simulated (What-If) or AI explanation. Alerts are patterns, not forecasts.
  • Data limits: NASA POWER is about 50 km resolution, so it describes the region, not one field. We show a confidence level and list information gaps, and SMAP covers only since 2015.
  • Farmer safety: the app never gives fertilizer or pesticide doses or product names. It points to soil tests, product labels and the extension office, and the chatbot refuses off-topic questions.
  • Accessibility: no account needed, mobile-friendly, simple wording, four languages, and color never used as the only signal.
  • Reliability and cost: free-tier cloud services, cached NASA data so repeat analyses are fast and the demo survives outages, and fallbacks when the AI or soil service is slow.
  • Privacy: no sign-up, no personal data collected, and farm analyses are not stored.
